newsitem.title: USA: Both major political parties court Louisiana voters.
newsitem.headline: Both major political parties court Louisiana voters.

text.p: Both major political parties are courting Louisiana's voters with everything but flowers to win the state's nine electoral votes, a U.S. Senate seat and a seat in the House of Representatives.

The presidential candidates have made repeated sorties into the state, alternating with appearances by their running mates and spouses. And national Democratic and Republican election committees are bolstering their candidates with a barrage of radio and television advertising.

"Louisiana has been doubly important this year as a swing state in both the presidential election and the U.S. Senate race," Louisiana State University political science professor Wayne Parent told Reuters.

"Never before has there been a competitive two-party battle for the U.S. Senate in Louisiana in a presidential election year. We got a lot of attention from the national parties in the '92 presidential election, but not like this."

Sen. J. Bennett Johnston, a Democrat, is retiring. Democratic former State Treasurer Mary Landrieu, a native of New Orleans, has a slight edge in the polls -- 41 percent to 37 percent -- over conservative Republican Woody Jenkins, a six-term state representative from Baton Rouge.

Landrieu, 40, pro-choice on abortion, is considered a moderate while Jenkins, 49, a former libertarian, has been an uncompromising anti-abortion leader and supports replacing the progressive income tax with a national sales tax.
In the South, the national Republican Party has targeted Louisiana as one of four states where it hopes to pick up Senate seats. The others are Arkansas, Alabama and Georgia.

Although there are two congressional races on the ballot, only one -- the 5th Congressional District in Monroe -- pits a Republican, physician John Cooksey, against a Democrat, state Representative Francis Thompson. Two Democrats, Chris John and Hunter Lundy, face off in the Nov. 5 election in the 7th District in southwest Louisiana.
Under the state's open primary system, all candidates run at the same time, regardless of party affiliation, with the top two vote-getters advancing to a runoff.

The 7th District was held by Republican Representative Jimmy Hayes, who gave up his seat in an unsuccessful bid for the Senate. Democratic Representative Cleo Fields lost his base when the federal courts redrew his district after deciding it had been racially gerrymandered to provide a black majority.
